title: The Pager

post.author: u/er_nights_gudrun
post.title: I'm a night doctor in an emergency department. At 02:30 our patient board showed a man I'd sent home, back in bay 4. The woman lying there had vanished from it.

blocks.text: I'm Gudrun, a doctor on nights in the emergency department at Pellingford General. We have 12 bays: curtained beds, numbered. A big screen at the desk shows who is in which bay, with the note a nurse writes when each patient arrives, called the triage note. That screen is the patient board.

Behind it, a computer elsewhere in the hospital keeps the board's list. Each patient is one line of that list, called a row, and each triage note is stored on its patient's row. Every hour, on the hour, the computer saves a copy of the whole list, so it can be put back if it breaks. That saved copy is a backup.

At 01:00, bay 4 held a man with chest pain that proved harmless. I sent him home at 01:10, and his row left the board. At 01:15 a woman with a broken hip took bay 4. At 01:20 the nurse wrote her triage note.

At 01:30 the board's makers sent a new version of its program, called an update. It had a fault: every time the program starts, it copies every row once. The program restarted, and every patient appeared twice. The copies carried no notes.

At night our engineers sleep at home with a pager, a small box that buzzes when the system needs a person. That buzz is a page. At 01:32 the board's alarm paged Jarlath. If nobody answers in 5 minutes, the page goes on to the next name, Breccan. Breccan answered at 01:39, Jarlath at 01:40. Neither was told about the other.
That is called being on call. Until tonight, the first name always answered in time, so one engineer worked each night problem alone. Tonight two logged in, and each picked a fix.

Jarlath chose a restore: wipe the live board, then load the 01:00 backup in its place. It takes about 14 minutes. Breccan chose a repair script: a short program that goes down the list and, where a patient appears twice, keeps the older row and deletes the newer one.

In our major-incident drills, one person takes charge, called the incident commander. Everyone reports to them before acting, and they keep the timeline: who did what, when. The engineers had no such rule.
Next day I pieced their timeline together. Each line shows the time, who acted, what they did, and to which data:

01:30  update   program restarts, copies every row  live board
01:44  Jarlath  starts restore from 01:00 backup     whole board
01:52  Breccan  runs repair script, keeps older row  live board
01:58  restore  finishes, program restarts          whole board
02:05  Breccan  runs repair script again            live board

At 01:52 Breccan's script left a clean board. At 01:58 the restore wiped it and put back the 01:00 list, and the restarting program doubled that. Breccan saw doubles again and reran his script. It kept the older rows: the 01:00 ones.
At 02:30 the board showed the man I'd sent home, back in bay 4.
The woman in bay 4 wasn't on it at all, and her triage note was gone. It fits: the man was in bay 4 at 01:00, so the backup had him; her note was written at 01:20, after it.
Each fix made sense alone. What should the hospital change before the next one?

blocks.label: bay_4_board_history.png

diagram.aria: 01:00 to 02:30 for bay 4 on the patient board. The man shows until he is sent home at 01:10, then shows again from 01:58 to 02:30. The woman shows from 01:15 until 01:58, then is off the board. Her triage note exists from 01:20 until 01:58, then is gone. Every patient shows twice from 01:30 to 01:52 and from 01:58 to 02:05. Jarlath's restore runs from 01:44 to 01:58. Markers: the update at 01:30, Breccan's script at 01:52, and his script again at 02:05.

blocks.caption: Bay 4, redrawn from the timeline. The man leaves the board at 01:10 and comes back at 01:58, when the restore puts back the 01:00 backup. The woman and her 01:20 note go at the same moment, because the backup was made before either existed. Breccan's script at 01:52 had cleared the doubles; the restore brought them back, and his second run at 02:05 kept the 01:00 rows.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Hospitals and engineers both rank problems by how bad they are. A problem bad enough to rank is an incident, and its rank is its severity; a board putting patients in the wrong beds is the top. So, questions. When Breccan ran his script at 01:52, who else was changing the board? Where could Jarlath and Breccan have heard each other? Who was writing the timeline while it happened, not the next day? And what did the board record between the backup and the update?

replies.author: u/er_nights_gudrun
replies.text: Jarlath was, with his restore; neither knew. They never spoke: each texted the desk on his own, and our nurse in charge thought they were one person. Nobody wrote a timeline until I did, the next afternoon. And between 01:00 and 01:30 the board recorded three things: the man going home, the woman arriving, and her note.

comments.author: u/sack_him_torsten
comments.text: Someone ran a script on live patient data without asking; that's a sacking, not a process. Breccan's second run is what made the 01:00 board stick. Take him off the rota, the list of who works which nights, and the next engineer will think twice before touching patient records at 2 AM.

comments.author: u/more_hands_oluf
comments.text: Two engineers for a top-severity night in an emergency department is thin. Page four. More people looking means more checks: someone would have walked the bays, or rung the desk, and spotted the man in bay 4 long before 02:30.

reply.prompt: The engineers will be paged again. What should the hospital change before the next bad night? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Name one incident commander, and let nobody change the board without their go-ahead.
options.part2: The hospital wrote one rule for every incident: the first engineer to answer is the incident commander, everyone reports in one shared channel, and nobody changes the board without the commander's go. We replayed the night in the sim with the rule on. Jarlath answered at 01:40 and took command. At 01:44 both plans came to him, and his timeline showed three changes since 01:00 that a restore would wipe, and an update still copying rows on every restart. His go: at 01:46 Breccan put back the previous version of the program, so it restarted without copying; at 01:52, Breccan's script, keeping the older row. The restore was held back. At 02:30: 9 rows, nobody shown twice, the woman in bay 4 with her 01:20 note, and the man nowhere on the board. One change at a time, all night.
options.senior: One person decides, so changes happen one at a time, in an order someone has thought about. The incident commander doesn't fix anything: they hold the timeline, hear every plan before it runs, and give the go. Responders report before acting, in one channel. Here that turned two good fixes that fought each other into a sequence: stop the cause, then repair, and keep the restore as a fallback.

options.text: Take the second engineer off the night rota, since his script made the bad restore stick.
options.verdict: Blame, and the gap stays open
options.part2: Breccan was moved to days. We replayed the night in the sim with Jarlath alone on the rota. His restore started at 01:44, finished at 01:58 and put back the 01:00 list, and the restart doubled it. Nobody ran a script. At 02:30 the board showed 18 rows: the man in bay 4, twice, and the woman and her note nowhere. Taking Breccan off removed the one fix that had worked, at 01:52. And the next night two engineers answer, they will meet the same gap.
options.senior: Blaming the last hand to touch the system feels like accountability, but it fixes nothing: the gap that let two changes run at once is still there, and the next pair will fall into it. Worse, people learn to hide what they did. A blameless post-mortem asks why the system allowed it, not who did it.

options.text: Page two more engineers on every serious incident, so there are more hands on the night.
options.part2: The hospital now pages four engineers for any top-severity incident. In the sim's replay all four answered and logged in. Jarlath restored, Breccan ran his script twice, and at 02:15 engineer 3 restarted the board program to clear the screen. The update was still installed, so it copied every row again. At 02:30: 18 rows, the man back in bay 4, the woman's note gone, and two changes running at once at 01:52, as before. More hands meant more changes, and still nobody choosing which went first.
options.senior: More responders without a commander means more changes at once, not more care. Paging more people helps only when someone gives them roles; otherwise each one finds something to do. Severity should decide who is told and how fast, and one commander should decide who acts.

options.text: Freeze the patient board until morning, and run the department on paper until it's fixed.
options.part2: The hospital froze the board at 01:44 and ran the department on paper. In the sim's replay the freeze held: the restore and both scripts were refused, the woman's note stayed on her row, and the man never came back. But the board froze doubled, 18 rows for 9 patients, wrong in front of everyone, and everything that happened from 01:44 went on paper at the desk, to be typed in by the day team. The doubles were never fixed, only stopped. The board is the department's record, and patients do not wait for morning.
options.senior: Freezing stops new damage, and a freeze of a few minutes while a plan forms can be right. Freezing until morning trades a broken board for no board, in a place where patients arrive every minute. The goal is a safe order of changes, not no changes.

sim.title: Run the night on Pellingford's patient board
sim.lede: You're the hospital's on-call lead, replaying last night from 01:00, one minute per tick, on a board of 12 bays. At 01:00 bays 1 to 9 are full, each patient one row with a triage note; bay 4 is the man. He goes home at 01:10, the woman takes bay 4 at 01:15, and her note is written at 01:20. At 01:30 the update makes the board program copy every row each time it starts. At 01:32 the alarm pages Jarlath; after 5 minutes the page goes on to Breccan. Jarlath's restore starts at 01:44 and takes 14 minutes; Breccan's repair script runs at 01:52, and again at 02:05 if he sees doubles. Pick an incident commander, who is on the rota, when each engineer acts, the restore point, the script's rule, and a freeze. With a commander, every plan is reported first and each change waits for his go.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run to 02:30 as built. Two changes at once at 01:52; at 02:30, 9 rows, the man back in bay 4, the woman's 01:20 note gone. Switch the restore to never: the 01:52 script alone leaves 9 rows and her note. Set the restore point to 00:00: two patients who went home are back. Now try each reply. Commander on: the update is put back at 01:46, the script runs at 01:52, and bay 4 shows the woman with her note. Jarlath only: 18 rows, the man twice in bay 4. Four engineers: engineer 3's restart at 02:15 doubles the board again. Freeze: her note survives on a board frozen with 18 rows. Last, keep the commander and set the script to keep the newer row: 0 notes.

explain.oneLine: Nothing on the board broke by itself. Two engineers, both paged for the first time at night, each made a sensible change alone. Jarlath's restore put back the 01:00 backup, which still had the man and never had the woman's note. Breccan's script, rerun at 02:05, made that hour-old list look clean. With nobody in command, two changes ran at once and the later one undid the earlier.

steps.title: How the call went out.
steps.text: First the board's alarm noticed doubles at 01:32 and paged the first engineer on call, Jarlath. Then, with no answer in 5 minutes, the page went on to the next name, Breccan; this step is called escalation. Then both answered, a minute apart, and logged in from home. Nothing told either one that the other was on. What can go wrong: escalation adds a person without adding a plan. Until tonight it had never fired at night, so the habits of one engineer working alone had never met a second engineer. Severity sets how loud and how wide the call goes, and a board putting patients in the wrong beds is the top.

steps.title: Two fixes, each sensible alone.
steps.text: A restore works in two steps: wipe what is there, then load a backup in its place. Everything written after the backup is lost, and the restore takes time, 14 minutes here, while the live board keeps changing. A repair script works on the live data: it reads every row, finds patients shown twice, keeps the older row and deletes the newer. Keeping the older row was right: the older row was the original, carrying the note. Breccan's script alone left a clean board at 01:52 (the sim shows it with the restore switched off). Jarlath's restore alone put back an hour-old list, and the faulty update doubled it.

steps.title: How they undid each other.
steps.text: At 01:52 the script removed the 9 copies, and the board was right. At 01:58 the restore, started before the script ran, finished and replaced the whole board with the 01:00 list: the man in bay 4, no woman, no 01:20 note. The program restarted and, with the update still installed, copied every row. At 02:05 Breccan saw doubles and ran his script again. It kept the older rows, which were now the 01:00 ones, and deleted the copies. The board looked clean, and was an hour old. Both changes touched the same data, and nobody knew both were running.

steps.title: One incident commander.
steps.text: In an incident, one person is named commander. They don't run fixes; they hold the picture. First, responders report each plan to the commander before acting, in one shared channel. Then the commander writes the timeline as it happens and decides the order of changes. Last, each change runs only on the commander's go. With the timeline in front of him, Jarlath would have seen three changes since the backup and an update still copying on every restart: stop the cause first, by putting back the previous version of the program, then repair, and keep the restore as a fallback. What can go wrong: a commander who starts fixing stops commanding, so command is handed over out loud when that has to happen. The hospital's major-incident drills use the same rule.

steps.title: The post-mortem: why, not who.
steps.text: After an incident the team writes a post-mortem: what happened, minute by minute, why, and what will change. A blameless post-mortem looks for the conditions that let it happen, not a person to punish. Here: why could two changes run on the board at once? Why did the restore not warn that it would wipe half an hour of records? Why did the update copy rows on every start, and why did it reach every bay at once? Each answer is a change to the system. Blaming Breccan answers none of them, and teaches the next engineer to keep quiet.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the next incident. The pager reaches the incident commander, Jarlath, who keeps the timeline. Every plan goes into one channel and is reported to the commander before anyone acts: the restore plan, held back as a fallback, and Breccan, who acts only on the commander's go. On the go, Breccan puts back the previous program at 01:46 and runs his script at 01:52, and the patient board ends with 9 rows and the woman in bay 4 with her note.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next incident. The first engineer to answer commands and keeps the timeline. Every plan goes into one channel and waits for a go. In the sim's replay: the previous program put back at 01:46, Breccan's script at 01:52, the restore held back, and at 02:30 a board of 9 rows with the woman in bay 4 and her 01:20 note.

fix.title: The fix: one commander, one channel, one change at a time
fix.text: Write one rule for every incident: the first engineer to answer is the incident commander until they hand it over out loud. Everyone who joins goes to one shared channel, says what they see, and reports any plan before acting. The commander writes the timeline as it happens, decides the order of changes, and gives each one a go; nobody changes the board without it. Severity decides who is paged and how fast. Afterwards, a blameless post-mortem asks why two changes could run at once and fixes that in the system. In the sim's replay: one change at a time, the update put back at 01:46, the script at 01:52, and the woman in bay 4 with her note at 02:30.

limits: A commander is one person. If they tire, or have to fix something themselves, command must be handed over out loud ("you have command"), or nobody has it.
The rule slows the first minutes: every plan waits for a go. For the top severity that is a few minutes well spent; small problems need a lighter rule.

It does not fix the update or the restore's blind spot. The post-mortem still has to make restores say what they will wipe, and make updates show their faults before every bay depends on them (Canary in the Mine).

head: Change
Good
Bad
rows: Fast: both fixes start within 20 minutes of the page.
Two changes at once; at 02:30 the man is back in bay 4 and her note is gone.
The restore alone: 18 rows at 02:30, the man twice in bay 4. The gap stays.
More hands for checks and calls.
A third change at 02:15 doubles the board again; the man back.
No further harm to the data; her note survives.
The board stays doubled; the department runs on paper all night.
One commander, changes on a go
One change at a time: 9 rows, the woman in bay 4 with her note.
Slower to start: every fix waits for the commander.

explain.seniorTake: An incident is a team sport with one captain. On-call and paging get people to the problem; severity decides how many and how fast. Once they arrive, the danger is no longer the fault but the fixes: two capable people changing the same data, each unaware of the other. Name one incident commander the moment someone answers. The commander does not fix: they hear every plan in one channel, write the timeline as it happens, choose the order, and give each change a go. Stop the cause before repairing, and keep big moves like a restore as a fallback, because a restore puts back everything the backup knew and nothing it didn't. Afterwards, run a blameless post-mortem that asks why the system let two changes run at once and turns each answer into a change. Firing the last hand to touch it only teaches the next one to stay quiet.

realWorld.title: GitLab, January 2017: one command on the wrong server
realWorld.text: GitLab's public post-mortem gives the moment, at about 23:30 UTC on 31 January: "an engineer proceeds to wipe the PostgreSQL database directory, errantly thinking they were doing so on the secondary." Then: "Unfortunately this process was executed on the primary instead." The primary was the live copy of the database; the secondary was its follower. GitLab's best estimate is that the loss "affected roughly 5,000 projects, 5,000 comments and 700 new user accounts."

realWorld.title: GitLab: backups that failed, a recovery in public
realWorld.text: "Unfortunately the process of both finding and using backups failed completely." GitLab worked in the open: "In the spirit of transparency we kept track of progress and notes in a publicly visible Google document", and it streamed the recovery on YouTube. Its fix aimed at the system, not the person: "Our main focus is to improve disaster recovery, and making it more obvious as to what host you're using; instead of preventing production engineers from running certain commands."

realWorld.title: Google SRE book: freelancing
realWorld.text: In "Managing Incidents" (written by Andrew Stribblehill, edited by Kavita Guliani), the unmanaged incident has an engineer who "was making changes to the system with the best of intentions. However, he didn't coordinate with his coworkers". The chapter's rule: "The operations team should be the only group modifying the system during an incident."

realWorld.title: Google SRE book: the incident commander
realWorld.text: "The incident commander holds the high-level state about the incident." The commander structures the response, "assigning responsibilities according to need and priority", and "De facto, the commander holds all positions that they have not delegated." And: "The incident commander's most important responsibility is to keep a living incident document."

realWorld.title: PagerDuty: the commander is not a resolver
realWorld.text: PagerDuty's incident response documentation says "An Incident Commander acts as the single source of truth of what is currently happening and what is going to happen during a major incident." Its duties include "Get everyone on the same communication channel", "Collect proposed repair actions and then recommend repair actions to be taken", and "Delegate all repair actions, the Incident Commander is NOT a resolver."

realWorld.title: PagerDuty: severity, and when unsure
realWorld.text: "If you are unsure which level an incident is (e.g. not sure if SEV-2 or SEV-1), treat it as the higher one." And: "During an incident is not the time to discuss or litigate severities, just assume the highest and review during a postmortem."

realWorld.title: Google SRE book: blameless postmortems
realWorld.text: In "Postmortem Culture" (written by John Lunney and Sue Lueder, edited by Gary O'Connor): "Blameless postmortems are a tenet of SRE culture." A postmortem "must focus on identifying the contributing causes of the incident without indicting any individual or team", because otherwise "people will not bring issues to light for fear of punishment."

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, A.5.24 to A.5.28: the incident controls
realWorld.text: Annex A of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 covers the life of an incident in A.5.24 to A.5.28: Information security incident management planning and preparation, Assessment and decision on information security events, Response to information security incidents, Learning from information security incidents, and Collection of evidence. The control wording is in the standard itself; the linked page is a secondary guide that lists them.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, A.5.27: learning from incidents
realWorld.text: A.5.27 is titled Learning from information security incidents: the post-mortem's job, written down as a control. The linked page is a secondary guide; the wording is in the standard.

realWorld.title: SOC 2 CC7.4: a defined incident response program
realWorld.text: SOC 2's common criterion CC7.4 reads: "The entity responds to identified security incidents by executing a defined incident response program to understand, contain, remediate, and communicate security incidents, as appropriate." One commander, one channel and a written timeline are what a defined program looks like at 01:40.

realWorld.title: GDPR Art. 32: restoring personal data in time
realWorld.text: Article 32(1)(c) of the GDPR asks for "the ability to restore the availability and access to personal data in a timely manner in the event of a physical or technical incident". A patient board is personal data about health, and a restore that brings back the wrong patients is not the availability it means.

asked: Walk me through how you'd run an incident.
What does an incident commander do?
interview.answer: First, someone notices: an alert pages the on-call engineer, and if they don't acknowledge in a few minutes it escalates to the next person. Whoever answers first declares an incident, sets a severity, and if unsure picks the higher one, which decides who else is paged and who is told. That first person is the incident commander until they hand it over explicitly. The commander doesn't fix things. They open one channel, get every responder into it, and ask each to report what they see and what they plan before they act. They keep a live incident document with a timestamped timeline, decide the order of changes, and give each one a go. They delegate roles: someone operating, someone communicating with the people affected, someone recording if it's big. A good order is: stop the bleeding by removing the cause, for example rolling back the bad release; then repair data carefully, ideally with a dry run; and keep heavy moves like a restore from backup as a fallback, because a restore loses everything since the backup. When it's over, write a blameless post-mortem within days: the timeline, impact, contributing causes and action items. Blameless means it looks for the conditions that allowed the failure, not a person to punish, because people who fear punishment hide what they did and the same failure comes back. A story I'd tell: a hospital's patient board started doubling rows after a bad update. Two on-call engineers joined at once without knowing about each other. One restored an hourly backup while the other ran a cleanup script on live data; the restore finished after the script and brought back an hour-old board, and the script's rerun made it look clean. A discharged patient reappeared and a triage note vanished. The fix wasn't firing anyone. It was one commander, one channel, and no change without the commander's go.

terms.def: The hospital in this story. Its emergency department has 12 bays and a patient board at the desk.
The part of a hospital that takes patients who arrive without an appointment, day and night. Also called the ER.
One curtained bed space in the emergency department, numbered 1 to 12 at Pellingford.
The big screen at the desk showing who is in which bay, with each patient's triage note. Staff trust it as the department's record.
The note a nurse writes when a patient arrives: what is wrong and how urgent it is. On the board it is stored on the patient's row.
One line in a stored list, for one thing: here, one patient on the board, with the bay, the time and the triage note.
A saved copy of data, kept so it can be put back if the live data breaks. Pellingford's board saves one every hour, on the hour.
A set of instructions a computer follows. The patient board is a program that reads the list of rows and shows it on the screen.
A new version of a program, sent to replace the old one. Tonight's had a fault: each time the program started, it copied every row.
Stopping a program and starting it again. With the faulty update installed, every restart of the board doubled every row.
A patient shown twice on the board: the original row and a copy. Tonight's copies carried the copy's time and no note.
At home but ready to work if needed, usually at night or weekends, like a doctor on call. Pellingford's engineers take turns.
A small device, or a phone app, that buzzes or rings when a system needs a person. The engineer on call carries it.
To send an alert to an on-call person's pager or phone so they act now. Every page should need a person to do something.
The board's automatic check that pages an engineer when something looks wrong. Tonight it saw doubles at 01:32.
Passing a page on to the next person when the first does not answer in time: 5 minutes at Pellingford. Tonight it sent the page to Breccan.
A problem bad enough to need people working on it now, with a severity, a commander and, afterwards, a post-mortem.
How bad an incident is, as a level: SEV-1 is the worst. It decides who is paged, how fast, and who is told.
A hospital's practice for a disaster, such as a bus crash, where one person takes charge and everyone reports to them.
The one person in charge of an incident. They decide the order of changes, give each a go, and keep the timeline; they don't do the fixing.
The list of who did what, when, during an incident, written as it happens. Gudrun's was pieced together the next day.
Putting back a backup in two steps: wipe the live data, then load the copy. Anything written after the backup is lost.
The moment the backup you restore was taken. Jarlath used 01:00; everything recorded after 01:00 was lost.
A short program written to do one job, often run by hand, like a written list of instructions for the computer.
Breccan's script: it reads every row, finds patients shown twice, keeps the older row and deletes the newer one.
The patient board's list as it is right now, the one staff are reading and writing, as opposed to a backup.
The list of who works which shift or which on-call night.
One shared place, such as a group chat or a call, where everyone working an incident talks, so each hears every plan.
The program as it was before the update. Putting it back, called a rollback, stopped the copying at 01:46 in the replay.
A plan kept in reserve, used only if the first plan fails. Here, the restore.
A written review after an incident: the timeline, what was hurt, why it happened, and what will change.
A post-mortem that looks for the conditions that let an incident happen, not a person to punish, so people speak openly.
Saying out loud that someone else is now incident commander ("you have command"), so there is never a moment with none.
PagerDuty's word for someone who does the fixing in an incident. The incident commander is not one.
The Google SRE book's name for the document the commander keeps up to date during an incident, with the timeline in it.
The Google SRE book's word for changing a system during an incident without telling the others working on it.
Running a script so it only reports what it would change, without changing anything.
A program that stores data in an organised way and finds it again on request, like a well-kept filing cabinet.
A computer whose job is to answer other machines' questions, like a clerk at a counter.
Two copies of a database: the primary takes every change, and the secondary follows it as a copy. GitLab wiped the primary by mistake.
A widely used free database program. GitLab.com ran on it in 2017.
A company that runs a website where programmers store and share their code. Its January 2017 outage post-mortem was public.
Short for Coordinated Universal Time, the world's reference clock. GitLab's timeline is in UTC.
Site reliability engineering: Google's name for engineers who keep large systems running, and the title of a book Google published about it.
A company that sells paging and on-call tools, and publishes its own incident response guide for free.
Severity 1, the worst level in PagerDuty's guide: a critical issue that warrants public notification.
A hands-on monitoring project on the site. Nightwatch N4 uses this case: you write an incident timeline.
An international standard for running information security. Its Annex A lists controls, including A.5.24 to A.5.28 on incidents.
An audit report, written by an outside checker, on a company's controls against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria.
A SOC 2 criterion: the company responds to security incidents with a defined incident response program, to understand, contain, fix and communicate them.
The EU's General Data Protection Regulation, the law on handling personal data. Article 32 covers keeping it secure and able to be restored.

atWork: Look for places where two responders can change the same system at once during an outage. It is a common pattern: two people join the same incident from different places, each picks a sensible fix, one restores while the other repairs by hand, and the second change quietly undoes the first. Check four things. Does every serious incident get one named incident commander, and does everyone know how to hand command over? Is there one channel that every responder joins before acting? Do changes during an incident wait for the commander's go, and is the timeline written as it happens? And do your post-mortems ask why the system allowed it, not who did it? Nightwatch N4 uses this case: you write an incident timeline for a monitored site. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, controls A.5.24 to A.5.28 cover incident planning, assessment, response, learning and evidence; if it is pursuing SOC 2, CC7.4 expects incidents to be handled under a defined incident response program, and its neighbours in CC7.3 to CC7.5 cover evaluating security events and recovering from incidents. Patient data on a board like this is personal data about health, and GDPR Art. 32 asks for the ability to restore it in a timely manner. Building the commander rule and a live timeline in now saves rework at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your company's web shop goes down at 22:00. Two on-call engineers answer the page. One starts rolling back yesterday's release; the other, separately, edits the live servers' settings by hand to speed them up. The rollback restarts every server and wipes the hand edits, so the second engineer edits again, and the shop flaps for an hour. What went wrong, and how would you run the next one?

keyIdeas.idea: Two people changed the same system at once without telling each other, and each change undid the other
Name one incident commander who decides the order and gives each change a go-ahead
Responders report in one channel before acting, and the timeline is written as it happens

recall.model: Two engineers changed the same system at once, without telling each other, and each change undid the other: the rollback overwrote the hand edits, so they were made again, and the shop flapped. Nobody knew both were running. Next time I'd name one incident commander as soon as the page is answered. The commander decides the order of changes and gives a go-ahead for each. Responders report before acting, in one channel, and the commander keeps the timeline as it happens. Here: finish the rollback first, check the shop, then tune the settings only if still needed, one change at a time.

recall.prompt: During an incident, what is the incident commander's job?
options: Runs the fixes personally, fastest hands first
Decides the order of changes, keeps the timeline, and gives each change a go
Writes the post-mortem and names who caused it
Pages every engineer on the rota
recall.why: The commander holds the picture and decides; others do the fixing. PagerDuty's guide says the commander is not a resolver, and the Google SRE book says the commander's most important job is a living incident document. At Pellingford, nobody held that role.

recall.prompt: A week after an outage, your manager drafts the post-mortem: "Root cause: an engineer ran the cleanup script on live data without asking. Action: remove the engineer from the on-call rota." What would you change in this post-mortem, and what should it ask instead?

keyIdeas.idea: Naming a person as the cause is blame; it fixes nothing, and people start hiding mistakes
Ask what in the system let it happen, such as two changes being able to run at once
Actions change the system: a commander's go-ahead for every change, dry runs, warnings before live data is touched

recall.model: Naming a person as the root cause is blame, and it fixes nothing: remove that engineer and the next engineer meets the same mistake, while everyone learns to hide what they did for fear of punishment. A blameless post-mortem asks why the system let two changes run at once, or what allowed a script to run on live data without a check: the contributing conditions. Then the actions change the system: an incident commander whose go-ahead every change waits for, one change at a time, and a dry run that shows what the script would change, with a warning before it touches live data.

recall.prompt: You can't tell whether an incident is severity 1 or severity 2. What does PagerDuty's guide say to do?
options: Treat it as the lower one until someone senior confirms
Wait until the cause is known, then choose
Treat it as the higher one, and review the level in the post-mortem
Leave it unrated so nobody is woken
recall.why: PagerDuty: "If you are unsure which level an incident is (e.g. not sure if SEV-2 or SEV-1), treat it as the higher one." Arguing about the level wastes the first minutes; the post-mortem can lower it later.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The commander rule has held through four incidents; no change runs without a go. Last night at 03:05 the board stopped saving. Only Jarlath answered. He named himself commander, then started the restore himself, watching it line by line. For 50 minutes nobody wrote the timeline and the desk heard nothing. Another engineer, paged at 03:10, joined at 03:20 and waited in the channel with no answer. The nurses, hearing nothing, wrote patients on the corridor whiteboard, and two bay moves never reached the board.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Jarlath followed the rule. What went wrong, and what should the rule add?

keyIdeas.idea: The commander also did the fixing, so nobody was commanding
When the second engineer joins, hand over command out loud, or give them the fix
Someone tells the department what is happening on a set rhythm, so the nurses know whether to trust the board

coldCase.model: Jarlath held both roles: he was commander and fixer at once, and a commander who is heads down in a restore has stopped commanding. PagerDuty puts it plainly: the commander is not a resolver. When the other engineer joined at 03:20, Jarlath should have done one of two things out loud: hand over command ("you have command, I'm restoring"), or delegate the restore and go back to commanding. Then someone has to tell the desk what is happening on a set rhythm, every 15 minutes, with a status even when nothing has changed, so the nurses know whether to trust the board or use paper. The rule should add: the commander does not fix, unless they hand over command first.
